messages.subject: Latent density per site
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently using unmarked to calculate snake density in three distinct areas (with slightly different size but roughly 1.5 ha each) throught removal models. I am using the multinompois function and  included the log-area of each site as an offset in the abundance formula to obtain the density. By doing so I obtained much better posterior probabilities for the resulting estimates than when no offset was included (from < 0.5 to > 0.6). However, the estimates were exactly the same as when no offset was included. Therefore, I would to ask you the following questions:

1) Is ranef producing density or abundance estimates?
2) If the estimates when including the offset of the log-area correspond to snake density, how is it possible that they are exactly the same as for the abundance model--i.e., when no offset is included.

Thank you in advance. If needed further details can be provided.

Best

Julien

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Standardizing observation covariates
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jena,

I think you need to standardize the full matrix with a single value for mean and sd. Standardizing by occasion/survey events would not make much sense in my opinion in your case.

In general I would always standardize with a single pair of mean and sd for a covariate. Exception might be something like day of year when modeling data from multiple years. If whatever affects detection, and which is correlated with date, varies quite a bit from year to year, then it might make sense to center date for each year on a separate value. Let's say you count some white species in some place where there is a snowcover in the winter. In that situation, you might center date in each year separately, by subtracting the average date of snowmelt from each date. A negative value of date then corresponds to a date when the landscape is still white, while a positive value means the white animals should be pretty visible in a brown or green landscape.

That is, by centering on snowmelt, you make date a much better proxy for what really matters for detection. (On the other hand, one could then also add a binary variable "pre- vs. post-snowmelt" into detection...).

Best regards  ---- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I would appreciate a bit of direction:
I have a data set that includes 3 years of point count data, but am struggling with how to decide the best way to analyze it. The faculty in my department cannot/will not offer any helpful guidance. Very thankful for this group!

Here is the structure of my data:
28 point count stations (250 meter radius; each point separated by 500m to avoid overlap)
We spatially distributed the listening stations (as best we could) to get 7 in each of 4 major cover types (these can/will be reworked to be continuous habitat covariates instead of 4 categories)
3 seasons (years; no hypotheses about differences between years in habitat config., mgmt, etc.)
3 visits per season (sometimes only 2 visits due to inclement weather)
Detections of several passerine spp. recorded to nearest meter and azimuth (I don't mind binning these into any number of discrete distance bands; the first detection only of each individual; successive vocalizations were ignored when it could be reasonable assumed it was the same individual)
We also recorded covariates that might affect detection rates (cloud cover, time since sunrise, et al. applicable data)
I understand the need to model each spp. separately, etc. with best fitting key fxns.
Q1: What I am mainly struggling with is the small myriad of ways to frame the data and subsequently analyze it. Can somebody recommend the "best" way to proceed? We are interested in density if possible, but realize that occupancy may be the fallback due to our medium-small sample size. I have played with these basic tutorials (https://darinjmcneil.weebly.com/), but find myself wishing the tutorials explained things a bit better...
Q2: How do you set up the analyses to incorporate separate years as well as the multiple visits/station?

I would greatly appreciate any advice or examples that closely mirror my sampling design. My main problem is that I absolutely love nitty gritty details of analyses, but I cannot help but overwhelm myself when it comes to making a final decision on which one to apply. I see too many viable options and no vignette I have found "looks like" my data.

Many thanks!
DM

Jena, good question, and Marc, thanks for your reply.

I have a similar situation - multiple surveys per year over multiple years, with day-of-year (DOY) included as an observation covariate.  I also included cumulative degree days as an observation covariate, as a continuous variable to measure the progress of spring.  However, our study subjects are amphibian egg masses laid in vernal pools, and the timing of egg-laying is likely a complex phenomenon, likely in some way related to degree days (soil, water, and air temps).  I've been including DOY to account for effects of spring's progress beyond thermal conditions which are captured in cumulative degree days.

Jena, if you know leaf-out correlates to cumulative degree days, this might perhaps be a better proxy and could be scaled across all years if I understand Marc correctly.

-Alex

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Choosing penalty value in occuMulti
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The answer to your first question is the optimizePenalty() function included in unmarked. It uses K-fold cross validation to determine which penalty is best from a set of possible penalties you provide. See ?optimizePenalty.

If you are comparing across multiple models and including penalties, you should not use AIC (which itself is a form of penalized likelihood). Instead you can use the same cross validation approach used by optimizePenalty for each combination of model and penalty term, and then choose the model/penalty combination with the highest overall cross validation score. Unfortunately unmarked does not have a built in function to do this specific task at the moment. I wrote a small function that returns the CV scores so they can be compared across models. See example below.

Thanks to Chris Rota for his input on this question.

Ken

----------

# Run first part of example in occuMulti help (?occuMulti) to get this fitted model
fit

set.seed(123)

# Find best value of penalty for a single model and re-fit the model with that penalty
# Uses k-fold cross validation
fit_opt <- optimizePenalty(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2))

# Compare models

# Fit a second model
newocc <- rep("~1", 7)
fit2 <- update(fit, stateformulas=newocc)

# Function to extract cross-validation score for each penalty value
# To get the CV score:
# 1. the dataset is divided into K folds of test/train data
# 2. For each fold, fit model with train data and penalty term
# 3. Using fitted coefficients from this model, calculate the sum of the site log-likelihoods for the test data
# 4. Sum across all K folds = final score (higher is better)
get_crossval <- function(object, penalties, k=5){
  folds <- unmarked:::partitionKfold(object, k)

  cvp <- sapply(penalties, function(p, k, fit, folds){
    cv <- sapply(1:k, function(i){
      refit <- update(fit, data=folds[[i]]$trainData, penalty=p, se=FALSE)
      sum(unmarked:::occuMultiLogLik(refit, folds[[i]]$testData))
    })
    sum(cv)
  }, k=k, fit=object, folds=folds)
  data.frame(model=deparse(substitute(object)), penalty=penalties, value=cvp)
}

# Get CV scores for a range of penalty values for each model
fit_scores <- get_crossval(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
fit2_scores <- get_crossval(fit2, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)

# Combine and sort. Max CV score = top model
# In this case for a given model the penalties all give very similar
# CV scores - not surprising since these simulated data don't really require penalized likelihood
results <- rbind(fit_scores, fit2_scores)
results[rev(order(results$value)),]

On Thu, 12 Jan 2023 at 23:59, Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:

> Hi,

> The answer to your first question is the optimizePenalty() function included in unmarked. It uses K-fold cross validation to determine which penalty is best from a set of possible penalties you provide. See ?optimizePenalty.
>
> If you are comparing across multiple models and including penalties, you should not use AIC (which itself is a form of penalized likelihood). Instead you can use the same cross validation approach used by optimizePenalty for each combination of model and penalty term, and then choose the model/penalty combination with the highest overall cross validation score. Unfortunately unmarked does not have a built in function to do this specific task at the moment. I wrote a small function that returns the CV scores so they can be compared across models. See example below.
>
> Thanks to Chris Rota for his input on this question.
>
> Ken
>
> ----------
>
> # Run first part of example in occuMulti help (?occuMulti) to get this fitted model
> fit
>
> set.seed(123)
>
> # Find best value of penalty for a single model and re-fit the model with that penalty
> # Uses k-fold cross validation
> fit_opt <- optimizePenalty(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2))
>
> # Compare models
>
> # Fit a second model
> newocc <- rep("~1", 7)
> fit2 <- update(fit, stateformulas=newocc)
>
> # Function to extract cross-validation score for each penalty value
> # To get the CV score:
> # 1. the dataset is divided into K folds of test/train data
> # 2. For each fold, fit model with train data and penalty term
> # 3. Using fitted coefficients from this model, calculate the sum of the site log-likelihoods for the test data
> # 4. Sum across all K folds = final score (higher is better)
> get_crossval <- function(object, penalties, k=5){
>   folds <- unmarked:::partitionKfold(object, k)
>
>   cvp <- sapply(penalties, function(p, k, fit, folds){
>     cv <- sapply(1:k, function(i){
>       refit <- update(fit, data=folds[[i]]$trainData, penalty=p, se=FALSE)
>       sum(unmarked:::occuMultiLogLik(refit, folds[[i]]$testData))
>     })
>     sum(cv)
>   }, k=k, fit=object, folds=folds)
>   data.frame(model=deparse(substitute(object)), penalty=penalties, value=cvp)
> }
>
> # Get CV scores for a range of penalty values for each model
> fit_scores <- get_crossval(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
> fit2_scores <- get_crossval(fit2, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
>
> # Combine and sort. Max CV score = top model
> # In this case for a given model the penalties all give very similar
> # CV scores - not surprising since these simulated data don't really require penalized likelihood
> results <- rbind(fit_scores, fit2_scores)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Matt,

the typical rationale of a goodness of fit (GOF) test is to see whether your data set looks similar to other data sets that you *could* have obtained under the specific assumptions of your model and assuming the parameter values estimated in your analysis. In a GOF test you calculate some discrepancy measure T which quantifies how different the observed data are from what the model says the data should look like, which is the 'expected values'. Examples for such functions T include Chisquared, Freeman-Tukey, sums of squares, deviance, and others. However, when you apply such a function T to your data and get some value, say t0=100, then what does it mean ? Does t0=100 indicate a fitting model or does it indicate a model that does not fit ?

For many classical GoF tests (often those leading to a Chisquared-distributed test statistic), there is theory that says that function T when applied to a data set has some known statistical distribution, so that you can then look up your value of t0=100 in a table of T and decide whether t0 is extreme under the Null hypothesis assumption of a fitting model. If your value t0 is extreme, then this means that it's unlikely under your model, and with the particular parameter values estimated, to get a data set such as yours. Hence, you conclude that your model and your data don't fit together well (and the data set wins...). In contrast, when you find that it is not unusual for a fitting model to produce a fit statistics T with a value of 100, then you say that your model fits the data and are happy ever after.

Now, in a parametric bootstrap you replace that distributional theory about T with raw computing power. That is, you *create* your own sampling distribution of the test statistic T under the Null hypothesis of a fitting model by using simulation. This then allows you to see how extreme your value t0 is in comparison to that sampling distribution of T (called t_B in unmarked). The parametric bootstrap does the following a large number of times:
Simulate a new (synthetic) data set under the parametric assumptions of your model and using the MLEs obtained in your analysis
Re-fit your model of interest to the synthetic data set
Calculate the chosen fit statistic T and save it
You repeat this typically 1000-10000 times and thus accumulate the empirical sampling distribution of the fit statistics T for a model that fits the data ... of course, the model fits since YOU chose a fitting model to simulate the synthetic data to begin with! Then, you can compare your t0 with the sampling distribution of t_B and do the same thing as in a classical GOF test where the distribution of t_B is known from statistical theory. That is, when t0 is extreme in view of its sampling distribution under the assumption of a fitting model, you reject the Null hypothesis and assume that the model doesn't fit your data set.

In your case, the top table compares the values of three fit statistics found for your data set (i.e., 157, 702 and 211) with their sampling distributions obtained by the parametric bootstrap. The last column tells you that it is not at all unusual to get such values of t_B under the Null hypothesis and hence, that your model fits when judged by the criterion of all three test statistics. The bottom table characterizes the three accumulated sampling distributions by their quantiles, so that you can see a little better where your values of t0 lie in comparison to the variation of the values that T may take on just by chance even for a fitting model.

About whether using these tests or the MacKenzie/Bailey test as implemented in AICcmodavg: it is possible that this latter test is more sensitive to violations of model assumption and hence better for GOF testing, I don't know. BTW, I don't think that in the MB test there is a problem with small counts since I believe its implementation is also based on a parametric bootstrap.

Best regards  --- Marc

PS: Bootstrapping is an incredibly powerful statistical method that ecologists should apply more in practice ...

first, I think the Wilkinson-Rogers notation for linear models in unmarked is pretty much the same as what you have in other R functions, including lm() and glm(). The following toy data allows you to check out what such models mean (in your case I think you get what you want):

# Simulate two factors

model.matrix(~trt-1)

model.matrix(~trt * region)                # Main effects and interaction
model.matrix(~trt + region + trt:region)   # same

model.matrix(~(trt-1):region)              # this is the same here, but again in a different parameterization

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Kellner,

Thank you for sharing this code & suggesting this method. Is there some threshold for the overall CV scores that indicates uncertainty in model selection, similar to <2 delta AIC? And does this overall CV method have any penalty for the number of parameters included in a model?

Thanks,
Leah

On Thursday, January 12, 2023 at 11:29:52 AM UTC-7 Ken Kellner wrote:
> Hi,
>
> The answer to your first question is the optimizePenalty() function included in unmarked. It uses K-fold cross validation to determine which penalty is best from a set of possible penalties you provide. See ?optimizePenalty.
>
> If you are comparing across multiple models and including penalties, you should not use AIC (which itself is a form of penalized likelihood). Instead you can use the same cross validation approach used by optimizePenalty for each combination of model and penalty term, and then choose the model/penalty combination with the highest overall cross validation score. Unfortunately unmarked does not have a built in function to do this specific task at the moment. I wrote a small function that returns the CV scores so they can be compared across models. See example below.
>
> Thanks to Chris Rota for his input on this question.
>
> Ken
>
> ----------
>
> # Run first part of example in occuMulti help (?occuMulti) to get this fitted model
> fit
>
> set.seed(123)
>
> # Find best value of penalty for a single model and re-fit the model with that penalty
> # Uses k-fold cross validation
> fit_opt <- optimizePenalty(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2))
>
> # Compare models
>
> # Fit a second model
> newocc <- rep("~1", 7)
> fit2 <- update(fit, stateformulas=newocc)
>
> # Function to extract cross-validation score for each penalty value
> # To get the CV score:
> # 1. the dataset is divided into K folds of test/train data
> # 2. For each fold, fit model with train data and penalty term
> # 3. Using fitted coefficients from this model, calculate the sum of the site log-likelihoods for the test data
> # 4. Sum across all K folds = final score (higher is better)
> get_crossval <- function(object, penalties, k=5){
> folds <- unmarked:::partitionKfold(object, k)
>
> cvp <- sapply(penalties, function(p, k, fit, folds){
> cv <- sapply(1:k, function(i){
> refit <- update(fit, data=folds[[i]]$trainData, penalty=p, se=FALSE)
> sum(unmarked:::occuMultiLogLik(refit, folds[[i]]$testData))
> })
> sum(cv)
> }, k=k, fit=object, folds=folds)
> data.frame(model=deparse(substitute(object)), penalty=penalties, value=cvp)
> }
>
> # Get CV scores for a range of penalty values for each model
> fit_scores <- get_crossval(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
> fit2_scores <- get_crossval(fit2, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
>
> # Combine and sort. Max CV score = top model
> # In this case for a given model the penalties all give very similar
> # CV scores - not surprising since these simulated data don't really require penalized likelihood
> results <- rbind(fit_scores, fit2_scores)
> results[rev(order(results$value)),]
>
>
> On Wed, Jan 11, 2023 at 02:01:10AM -0800, Divyajyoti Ganguly wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > There is a 'penalty' argument in function occuMullti (package unmarked). If

> > I am not sure how to go about choosing which value of penalty to retain in
> > my models. Some leads on this would be helpful.
> >

> > the models of the model set? Or, should it be added only to those models
> > that produce large estimates? I tried both, but in the latter case it is
> > resulting in huge differences in the AIC between the penalised models
> > (complex) and the non-penalised models from the same model set.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jamie,

Regarding relative importance( ), you need to use the parm argument to
specify the variable name as it appears in the model output. For
example, if you have a Habitat variable with A, B, and C levels, you
could then write importance(parm = "HabitatB"), depending on the
reference level that was used in your model. This being said,
importance values are a "semi-quantitative" measure and can be of
limited value: you still need to inspect the output of the models
carefully, as a variable with high importance values might be
hitchhiking a ride in a model with a good predictor. Instead, you could
look at model-averaged predictions across your models vs the predictor
of interest.

Regarding evidence( ), the function requires the model selection table
as input.

Here is an example below illustrating both using an unmarked data set:

require(unmarked)
##single season example modified from ?occu
data(frogs)
pferUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin)
##add fake covariates
siteCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF)),
                                sitevar2 = runif(numSites(pferUMF)))

##observation covariates
obsCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF) *
                               obsNum(pferUMF)))

##basic model set
fm1 <- occu(~ obsvar1 ~ sitevar1, pferUMF)
fm2 <- occu(~ 1 ~ sitevar1, pferUMF)
fm3 <- occu(~ obsvar1 ~ sitevar2, pferUMF)
fm4 <- occu(~ 1 ~ sitevar2, pferUMF)

##assemble models in named list
CandMods <- list("fm1" = fm1, "fm2" = fm2, "fm3" = fm3, "fm4" = fm4)

##model selection table
modTable <- aictab(cand.set = Cand.mods, second.ord = TRUE)

##evidence ratio
evidence(modTable)

##relative importance of sitevar1
importance(cand.set = Cand.mods,
           parm = "sitevar1", parm.type = "psi")

Hope it helps,

Marc

two models you want to compare. The default compares the top vs 2nd-
ranked model, but you can choose whichever pair of models you want.

model selection table for the model names to use.

In your example of modavg( ), you should specify parm.type = "detect"
if your predictor is on detection probability. To get predictions, you
can use modavgPred( ).

Marc

messages.subject: AHM workshop @Patuxent, 17-21 July 2023
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Ken Kellner, Andy Royle and I will run an AHM workshop at what used to be the glorious Patuxent Wildlife Research Center in Laurel, MD, during 17-21 July 2023. We will show how to use likelihood and Bayesian methods to fit a large range of models that are useful for investigations of abundance and occupancy. Planned topics include:
Occupancy models for binary detection/nondetection data
Binomial N-mixture models for replicated count data
Multinomial N-mixture models for replicated capture-recapture data
Distance sampling models for a variety of distance sampling protocols
Modeling of false positives
Integrating multiple data types and integrated models

Please send your application to Andy Royle (aro...@usgs.gov), with CC to marc...@vogelwarte.ch and kell...@msu.edu, and describe your background and knowledge in statistical modelling, R and JAGS/Nimble, and occupancy/Nmix models, by 30 April 2023.

You find some more information in the attached flier.

Best regards --- Marc, Ken and Andy

messages.subject: Re: Plotting predict() with scaled covariates but not having the x-axis scaled
messages.subject_clean: Plotting predict() with scaled covariates but not having the x-axis scaled
messages.body_plain:
There are two ways to approach this.

1. Instead of standardizing your covariates ahead of time, have unmarked do the work for you by putting scale() in the formulas, e.g.

occu(~scale(area)~scale(road), umf).

Then when using predict, supply the newdata on the original (non-standardized) covariate scale, and combine the newdata and the results from predict when making the plot.

2. If you standardize the covariates yourself first, as you have done, it's a little harder. After fitting the model, create a covariate range to plot (x), on the original scale. Then standardize this range *using the same values for the mean and SD used to standardize the original dataset*. Supply the standardized range of values x_scaled to the predict newdata argument. Then plot the results of predict (y) vs. the original covariate range (x). If you have other non-focal covariates in the model you are holding constant, you need to standardize them the same way before putting them in the newdata, using the mean and SD values from the original dataset.

Ken
